newsitem.title: USA: Motorola outlook positive but cautious, stock falls.
newsitem.headline: Motorola outlook positive but cautious, stock falls.

text.p: Technology giant Motorola Inc. has begun its recovery after battling with stiff competition in its key seminconductor and cellular phone businesses but analysts cautioned Tuesday that a rebound will be gradual.
"I think we're at the beginning of a new cycle for them in wireless (phones) and semiconductors," said Mona Eraiba, an analyst for investment bankers Gruntal & Co.

Motorola, based in Schaumburg, Ill., surprised Wall Street late Monday with better-than-expected first quarter results. But Motorola's stock still came under pressure Tuesday, falling $1.25 to $59 on the New York Stock Exchange.

"It's a second-half story, and that's exactly what I think people are waiting for, but in this market there is very little patience," said Douglas Christopher, an analyst for investment bankers Crowell, Weedon & Co.

Motorola reported first-quarter earnings of $325 million or 53 cents a share, including gains on the settlement of a patent suit and the sale of an investment, vs. year-ago earnings of $384 million or 63 cents a share. Despite the decline, the earnings were still above analysts' expectations of 45 cents a share.
Motorola's sales were $6.6 billion, down from nearly $7 billion in last year's first quarter, and the company said the drop was largely attributable to its semiconductor business.
The worldwide semiconductor industry, which has been plagued with overcapacity and pricing pressures, saw its total revenues last year drop by 9 percent, Motorola said.
In a conference call with analysts, Motorola said it expected the computer chip industry to grow in 1997 by about 10 percent compared with 1996, but called the recovery "very gradual."

"We continue to expect a modest rate of recovery for the industry and our semiconductor business with all the year-over-year growth in the second half of 1997," said Ed Gams, chief of Motorola'a investor relations.
In its cellular phone infrastructure business, which includes so-called base stations and network equipment, Motorola said it was well positioned for future growth.
Motorola said the cellular phone unit's infrastructure backlog increased during the first quarter, but most of those orders were scheduled for delivery later in 1997 and in the first quarter of 1998.
"Consequently, cellular infrastructure sales in the second quarter of 1997 may only exhibit modest growth vs. the prior year," Gams said.

In cellular phones, where competition and a switch to digital technology has meant a loss of market share for Motorola, the company had higher sales but a slight drop in orders from a year ago. Motorola said the decline was due principally to lower sales in Korea and Japan.
The company said it launched an entire new line of digital cellular phones based on so-called GSM (global system for mobile communications) technology.

It also plans to introduce new products this summer based on another kind of digital technology known as CDMA (code division multiple access). The new CDMA phones use Motorola's own chip sets, while Motorola's current CDMA phones use Qualcomm Inc. semiconductors.
"Our new CDMA subscriber products, based on this chip set, are expected to provide the opportunity to recover market share in these two countries beginning later in 1997," Gams said.
"It's going to be slow going for another quarter or so," Lawrence Borgman, an analyst with investment bankers Josephthal, Lyon & Ross, said of the cellular division.

Motorola said it would continue to take steps to restore growth in profits and revenues, which may result in charges against earnings later in the year. But Gams said it was too early to give specific information about the steps and possible charges.
"Steps taken in several business segments last year to reduce costs are beginning to have a favourable impact," Motorola President Robert Growney said.
In last year's fourth quarter, Motorola took pre-tax charges totalling more than $150 million related to cost cutting measures, including job cuts.
"We are committed to restoring Motorola's long-term pattern of growth in profits and revenues," Christopher Galvin, chief executive of Motorola, said in a statement.
